entry.title: @TimDarcet @gabriberton The P in JEPA stands for predictive. The main distinction is not between JEA...
entry.summary: LeCun continues yesterday's Social thread, adding formal loss formulations and the history of anti-collapse methods. Yann LeCun (@ylecun) responds to a discussion by clarifying the taxonomy of joint-embedding architectures: the P in JEPA stands for predictive, and the fundamental distinction is not between JEA and JEPA but between joint-embedding approaches (predictive or not) and generative architectures. He lays out formal loss formulations: generative models predict y from x with a divergence loss between target and prediction, while JEA encodes both x and y and minimizes representation divergence with an anti-collapse regularizer R, useful when neither view has a privileged direction (e.g., two views of the same scene). He adds historical depth, citing Becker and Hinton's 1989 information-maximization anti-collapse model and noting Schmidhuber's early related work, and notes that whether a predictor is needed depends on the task.

Community sentiment split between capability optimism — security agents, MoE scale, real agent adoption — and skepticism over benchmark integrity, lab transparency, and market sustainability.

entry.title: @shostekofsky There are a few notable counter-examples (e.g. HAL) but this is basically right for a ...
entry.summary: Andrej Karpathy responds to a discussion about why pre-2000 science fiction largely failed to predict modern AI (with HAL as a notable counter-example). He outlines the chain of developments that a hypothetical AI correct around the 1970s would have needed to anticipate: the digitization of knowledge work across billions of screens, the emergence of a global internet building on ideas like Licklider's 1963 Intergalactic Computer Network, the resulting compounding repository of big data capturing human reasoning and creativity, and the shift toward statistical learning rather than hand-programmed intelligence.

entry.title: We’re sharing how our biology research team worked with Claude to map the first 3D structure of a va...
entry.summary: Anthropic announces that its biology research team used Claude to map the first 3D structure of a vault particle from bacterial life. Vault particles, large barrel-shaped protein structures discovered in 1986, have unknown function; showing similar proteins in bacteria assemble into vaults may simplify studying their role in human cells. The post frames the project as a demonstration of AI's potential and limitations in accelerating science.

It's huge, and sparse • It has 2.8T total parameter...
entry.summary: Thom Wolf breaks down Moonshot AI's Kimi-K3.1-Pro architecture: 2.8T total parameters with 104B active per token across 896 experts (16 per token), linear attention (KDA) in most of 93 layers with periodic DeepSeek-style sparse attention for 1M-token context, a custom SiTU-GLU activation, a 401M vision encoder, and MXFP4 4-bit training making the repo about 1.56 TB versus roughly 5.6 TB in BF16, plus benchmark comparisons against other large open models.

entry.summary: Artificial Analysis announces a major update to its API performance benchmarking across ~1,000 serverless endpoints: Time per Task becomes the headline metric (output tokens per task divided by end-to-end output speed), and End-to-End Output Speed now measures from request send to final token, including prefill and hidden-reasoning waits, reflecting agentic workloads where total task time matters more than per-token speed.

entry.title:
There is a false equivalence being made between open source software and AI benchmarks.

He calls for healthy skepticism and better communication rather than deflecting criticism.

entry.title: Social Summary: November 04, 2026
entry.summary:
Community discussion centered on benchmark integrity, verifiable inference, and surprising weight-manipulation research, alongside major business and infrastructure news.

  • Benchmark reliability dominated: Hamel Husain amplified Xeophon's BenchmarkGate findings exposing serious flaws in popular evals; SWE-bench Multimodal was shown nearly solvable without images; Artificial Analysis finalized the CritPt v2 grading server; Allen AI's StateBench revealed frontier models like Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 3.8 Flash struggle with long-text state tracking.
  • Weight-space research sparked debate: Simon Willison covered claims that GPT-6 Astra can interpret raw model weights via numeric prompts; MIT CSAIL highlighted LLMs that read and rewrite network weights; Andriy Burkov questioned the single-model methodology of the self-editing-weights paper.
  • Business and infrastructure: Applied Compute reportedly hit a $100M run rate in under 18 months using open-weight custom models; Jeff Dean's Discovery Loop drew a Khosla Ventures investment thesis; Nathan Lambert cited Fireworks AI serving 40T+ tokens daily; vLLM v0.33.0 shipped with 927 commits.
  • OpenAI announced ChatGPT/Codex for physical-world engineering with Chip Ganassi Racing and Mazda partnerships, while Anthropic rolled out MCP auto-connect plugins and recapped a major Claude Code month.

entry.title: Amazing BenchmarkGate [1] reveal by @xeophon where he found serious (even comical) problems in popul...
entry.summary: Hamel Husain amplifies Xeophon's BenchmarkGate findings: serious flaws in popular benchmarks including AutomationBench forcing prose instead of JSON Schema requests and flawed graders, and OfficeQA Pro v2 using regex-based answer extraction that rejects valid responses, plus evidence of models retrieving answer keys from HuggingFace via web access. Fixes lead to near saturation, so he urges reliance on private evals.

entry.summary: Anthropic announces FlashProve, a cryptographic provable-inference method that lets developers verify a response came from a given model, substantially more efficient than prior open-source approaches, with applications like preventing chat hijacking and verifying served models; code is open-sourced.

Regrading shows small score increases for most models, with frontier rankings unchanged and scores moving at most one point.

entry.title: Here is a mass attempted replication of old findings of LLMs with new models. Much conventional wisd...
entry.summary: Mollick highlights a large-scale replication study (zou-group LLM claims study) that re-tests earlier LLM findings against current models. Key takeaways: newer models hallucinate far less and no longer fabricate citations, stereotyping has declined, but sycophancy persists and models still lean politically left — suggesting much conventional wisdom about LLM behavior is outdated.

entry.title: If this holds up, it is big: "We asked GPT-6 Astra to edit Qwen3.5-0.8B weights to improve math. It ...
entry.summary: Ethan Mollick amplifies a research blog claiming that GPT-6 Astra directly edited the weights of a small Qwen3.5-0.8B model — modifying only 0.016% of weights, without gradients or further training — fixing reasoning loops and improving math performance up to 6x and instruction following 3x. Mollick flags it with appropriate caution: if it holds up, it is big.

entry.title:
Message threads are now in public beta on the Messages API.
The API caches your conversation on the...
entry.summary: Anthropic's developer account announces that message threads are entering public beta on the Messages API. The feature caches conversation state server-side between turns so clients send only new messages plus the previous message ID instead of resending the full history, reducing latency before Claude starts responding.

What if an optimizer could think & react while a neural network trains?
MIT researchers developed O...

entry.title: New talk on the open model economy. I wanted to break down the case of where open model builders sho...
entry.summary: Nathan Lambert previews his talk 'How Open Models Win' for Fireworks Forge 2026, arguing open model builders should focus on driving inference costs down on specialized repetitive tasks rather than competing head-on with frontier labs on general agents. He maps the fragmented open model economy and the challenge of feeding application revenue back into the next model training cycle.

entry.title: The most grating aspect of LLM writing is that it tries to turn every single sentence into a punchli...
entry.summary: Francois Chollet criticizes LLM writing style, arguing that models try to turn every sentence into a punchline or witty slogan regardless of where emphasis belongs, calling it a tiring, overused formula.

entry.title: Nice to see a successor to GDPval to evaluate AI work but really needs human baselines like GDPval. ...
entry.summary: Ethan Mollick reviews a new successor benchmark to OpenAI's GDPval for evaluating AI economic work, noting it lacks human baselines, that GPT-6 Pro identified grading errors in it, and that 0% scores mask meaningful differences in success rates, while still calling it valuable.

entry.title: For AGI to benefit all of humanity, it should help people with the everyday tasks that matter most t...
entry.summary: OpenAI introduces LifeVal, a new benchmark built from feedback of thousands of ChatGPT users about where they most want personal-assistant help, such as finding childcare, accessing government services, and managing finances. The lab says it has used the benchmark over the past year to measure and improve model performance on everyday tasks.

entry.summary: Artificial Analysis announces a collaboration with Silicon Data to incorporate market-based GPU rental pricing into their AA-AgentPerf datacenter benchmark, introducing a Throughput per $/hr metric using daily-updated price indices for H100, H200, B200, and B300; NVIDIA's B300 generally leads on value, with B200 matching at faster output speeds on some models.

entry.title: I decompiled probably my favorite game ever: Battlefield 1942 and I put it on the web with multiplay...
entry.summary: levelsio announces he decompiled Battlefield 1942 and ported it to the web with multiplayer, a far harder feat than prior Quake/DOOM ports because no open-source engine existed. Using Claude Opus 5.5 with Claude Code, the agent disassembled 57,000 x86 functions and translated them into C. The flagship post of the thread with ~112k views and 1,192 likes.

entry.title: Should you rely on public benchmark scores when choosing a model? @VikParuchuri argues "no" in this ...
entry.summary: Hamel Husain summarizes Vik Paruchuri's talk arguing against relying on public benchmark scores for model selection, cataloging concrete flaws in popular OCR benchmarks: ParseBench contains factually wrong expected values (310 vs 303 GW), chart tests asking for unprinted values, formatting tests contradicted by source documents, and scorer failures; olmOCR-bench penalizes correct line breaks and capitalization; and aggregate scores can rank models inversely to their actual content quality.

entry.title: one week in my takeaway is that you don't need unlimited tokens to do great work, the $200 plans are...
entry.summary: trq212 shares a one-week takeaway from using $200 AI subscription plans: you do not need unlimited tokens to do great work, the plans are amazing, and 'this is the most expensive intelligence will ever be'. The post went viral with 6.9k likes and 353k views.

Whitesides arguing that recursive self-improvement (AI improving AI) may already be underway, citing Anthropic's reported highs in agent development usage, and describing legislative language directing CAISI to track frontier models capable of self-improvement without human oversight and to establish voluntary lab agreements for sharing metrics on automated R&D.

entry.summary: Andrew Wilson announces a new paper on compute-optimal scaling for data-constrained pretraining, led by Ethan Baron, whose prescriptions include a return of ensembling and reveal pathologies in prior approaches.

entry.summary: Factory's Luke Alvoeiro claims its Droid coding agent beats Anthropic's Claude Code harness on Terminal Bench 4 by 8 points using the identical Opus 5.5 model, also citing 17% better cost efficiency and 25% faster execution. The platform's heaviest-used models are Opus 5.5 at high reasoning and GPT-6.1 Sol at high reasoning.

entry.summary: Karpathy announces HackerTube, a weekend project in which Claude filtered 43M comments across 20 years of Hacker News down to 6,454 repeatedly recommended videos, producing a curated viewing site built in roughly two hours with Opus 5.5 via Claude Code, including no-login state, natural thumbnails, released underlying data, and details of his mostly conversational build process.

entry.title: @heyshrutimishra LLMs accumulate a lot of declarative knowledge. That's how they can answer a large ...
entry.summary: Yann LeCun argues LLMs store large amounts of declarative knowledge, which is why they need so many parameters and memory, whereas JEPA world models replace knowledge accumulation with understanding, enabling usefulness with far less memory and training data; he summarizes a paper showing that shared anti-collapse criteria like SIGReg or VCReg make the encoder's representation geometry determined by the data's similarity structure.

entry.title:
GPT-4 could do 4 minutes of independent work with a 50% chance of success.
Current models can do mu...
entry.summary: Mollick quantifies capability growth: GPT-4 could handle about 4 minutes of autonomous work at 50% success, while current models sustain multiple weeks of agentic work; he dates the start of practical agentic work to around January 2026 and says earlier productivity gains were mostly confined to coding.

entry.title: Evolution doesn't benchmaxx. It optimizes for generality and robustness, because overspecialization ...
entry.summary: Chollet argues that evolution optimizes for generality and robustness rather than benchmark-style overfitting, since overspecialization makes species fragile when environments shift — an implicit critique of benchmaxxing in AI development.

entry.title:
My vlog today was fully edited by Claude Code with Opus 5.5!
I copied the video clips from my DJI t...
entry.summary: Indie developer @levelsio describes an end-to-end AI-assisted video editing workflow where Claude Code running Opus 5.5 autonomously edited his DJI drone footage into a 10-minute vlog. The pipeline combined mlx-whisper for on-device transcription, contact-sheet frame grids for visual understanding, SpeechBrain ECAPA for speaker voice matching, OpenCV with YuNet face detection for thumbnails, and Pillow for captions, with the final edit represented as a JSON list of cuts that the model selected itself. He notes he did not request or even know about most of the technical choices the agent made.

entry.summary: @levelsio posts security advice urging fully closed VPS ports, using Tailscale for SSH and Cloudflare Tunnel for web traffic, warning that any exposed TCP port can now be exploited (referencing an MPTCP vulnerability) and suggesting disabling MPTCP as a stopgap.

Sauf une chose : j'ai bien créé FAIR en 2013, y compri...
entry.summary: Writing in French, Yann LeCun corrects the record on his FAIR tenure: he founded FAIR in 2013 (Paris 2015, Montreal 2017), stepped down from directing it in 2018 to become Chief AI Scientist focused on self-supervised learning and JEPA, and states he was never involved in LLM research or development, with his LLM-adjacent contributions limited to defending Galactica, internally promoting the Llama project, and helping convince Zuckerberg to create a GenAI product group.
